# Green does not mean live: what changed in v1.1.0

2 unchanged paragraphs

Two consecutive releases of this site pushed cleanly, verified themselves against both remotes, printed **"both remotes in sync —sync, done"**, and never reached anybody. The site served a two-release-old page for forty minutes. It was noticed by a human on a phone, who looked at the version badge and said *"is this the latest version?"*

3 unchanged paragraphs, under What the release actually verified

1. Build the site from source. 2. Run the validator —validator, structure, links, markdown twins, orphan pages, and a tripwire that scans every tracked file for a vault key. 3. Commit and push the encrypted vault; confirm `sgit status` reports in sync. 4. Commit and push the git mirror; confirm `HEAD == origin/dev`.

Step 4 is where the confidence came from, and it is genuinely a strong check —check, it compares hashes, not hopes. The problem is what it means. It means **the bytes arrived at GitHub**. It does not mean anybody can read them.

5 unchanged paragraphs, under The gap, named, What actually failed

Not our code. Not the content. The deploy job died in **"Set up job"** —job"**: before running a single step of its own:

7 unchanged paragraphs, under The fix is one question, asked at the end

The cost is real: up to eight minutes of waiting on every release. We took it, because the alternative had already been demonstrated twice in one afternoon —afternoon, telling somebody a fix was live when it was not, twice, in writing.

2 unchanged paragraphs, under The rule underneath

• **A page nothing links to is unpublished.** The build fails on an orphan page —page, it happened once, a brief that was written, built and pushed while nothing linked to it.

• **A page the machine index omits is unpublished.** The build fails if any page would be missing from `llms.txt` —`llms.txt`, that happened too, a whole section silently absent.
